analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal oil tax that funds toxic waste site cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 16.4-cents-per-barrel petroleum Superfund tax never got a hearing or a vote, dying in the Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 — so the tax remains in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal excise tax on oil — 16.4 cents per barrel, adjusted yearly for inflation — that Congress reinstated in 2022 to pay for cleaning up the nation's worst toxic waste sites through the Hazardous Substance Superfund. It would also end the Treasury's authority to advance money to that fund, effective immediately. In practice it would be a tax cut for oil producers, refiners, and importers, with the savings at the gas pump amounting to well under a penny per gallon. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Oil producers, refiners, and importers of petroleum products would gain the most, since they pay the 16.4-cents-per-barrel tax on crude oil and imported petroleum products. Drivers would see at most a fraction of a penny per gallon in savings (a barrel is 42 gallons). Companies responsible for contaminated sites would benefit indirectly from a weaker cleanup fund. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the excise tax on domestic crude oil and imported petroleum products (16.4 cents per barrel, indexed for inflation) retroactive to January 1, 2023, cutting a cost currently borne by the oil industry and, at the margin, by consumers at the pump.
Ends the Treasury's authority to advance general tax revenue to the Hazardous Substance Superfund, which currently runs through 2032, by terminating the funding stream rather than replacing it.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers and the communities near the nation's most contaminated sites. The Superfund tax is the dedicated revenue for cleaning up hazardous waste sites; repealing it would shift that cleanup burden from oil companies onto the Treasury's general fund — or leave cleanups without dedicated money at all. The tax's repeal would be retroactive to January 1, 2023, which would also require refunding taxes already collected. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

drawbacks.text: The pump-price benefit is negligible: 16.4 cents per barrel spread over 42 gallons is about four-tenths of a cent per gallon, so consumers would gain almost nothing while the cleanup fund loses its dedicated revenue.

The Hazardous Substance Superfund, which pays for remediating contaminated sites, would lose both its tax revenue and its authority to receive Treasury advances through 2032, shifting cleanup costs from oil companies to general taxpayers or leaving sites unfunded.
The repeal would be retroactive to January 1, 2023, forcing the government to refund taxes already collected since the current rate took effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to ordinary people is tiny — well under a penny per gallon even if oil companies passed the full savings through — while its cost is the loss of the dedicated, polluter-pays funding stream for cleaning up the country's worst toxic waste sites. As designed, it is essentially an oil-industry tax cut dressed up as pump-price relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in May 2023 and sat there without a hearing or a vote until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Carey introduced the bill on May 25, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax bills.
Eight House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — ever appears in its history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee, leaving the petroleum Superfund tax enacted in 2022 in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public and communities that depend on Superfund cleanups came out ahead: because the bill died, the 16.4-cents-per-barrel tax keeps flowing into the Hazardous Substance Superfund instead of being repealed. Oil companies did not get the tax cut.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities relying on Superfund cleanup funding

for.name: Rep. Mike Carey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the petroleum Superfund tax and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 8 of 226 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from May 2023 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only visible support was the Republican sponsor and 8 Republican cosponsors, with no Democrats attached and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and petroleum importers
industries.note: The bill would repeal the 16.4-cents-per-barrel excise tax these companies pay on domestic crude and imported petroleum products — the sole dedicated funding for the Hazardous Substance Superfund. Their tax cut would come at the expense of the cleanup fund that addresses contamination in the petroleum supply chain. Because the bill died, they pay the tax still.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other parties responsible for contaminated sites
industries.note: A weaker Superfund means less money to remediate hazardous waste sites, easing the broader funding environment around cleanup obligations. Their direct cleanup liability would not change, but the dedicated fund backing remediation would be gone.
